instrument: Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China (Art. 20, inserted 2025)
original_title: 中华人民共和国网络安全法（第二十条）
ai_systems_covered: AI generally, through a new state-policy article on AI research, infrastructure, ethics and safety supervision; AI is not defined
regulatory_trigger: None for firms: the article directs state action; the amendment, including Art. 20, has applied since 1 January 2026
core_duties: Risk management
enforcement_authority: The national cyberspace department coordinates, with telecommunications, public security and other State Council departments, under the Law generally
remedy_or_sanction: No sanction attaches to Art. 20; the amendment raised the Law's general fines to as much as RMB 10 million for the most serious breaches (Arts. 61, 69)
identified_gap: The AI article is promotional: it places no enforceable duty or liability on developers or deployers, so it signals policy direction without adding operative AI obligations.
source_citation: Decision of the NPC Standing Committee on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China (adopted 28 October 2025, President's Order No. 61, in force 1 January 2026), new Art. 20

instrument: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China
original_title: 中华人民共和国个人信息保护法
ai_systems_covered: Automated decision-making using personal information, defined in Art. 73(2); AI itself is not defined
regulatory_trigger: Processing personal information, including for automated decision-making or personalised push and marketing
core_duties: Transparency; Impact assessment; Audit; Data governance
enforcement_authority: The CAC coordinates; State Council departments and local governments enforce within their remits (Art. 60)
remedy_or_sanction: Rectification, warning, confiscation and app suspension, with fines up to RMB 1 million on refusal to rectify; in serious cases up to RMB 50 million or 5% of prior-year turnover (Art. 66); presumed-fault damages (Art. 69)
identified_gap: The Art. 24 explanation and refusal rights apply only to decisions with an undefined 'major impact', the refusal right only to decisions made solely by automated means, and there is no express right to human review, so most partly automated decisions escape them.
source_citation: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China (adopted by the NPC Standing Committee 20 August 2021, President's Order No. 91, in force 1 November 2021), Arts. 24, 55, 73(2)

instrument: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendation in Internet Information Services
original_title: 互联网信息服务算法推荐管理规定
ai_systems_covered: Services using generation/synthesis, personalised push, ranking, search/filtering or scheduling/decision algorithms to supply information (Art. 2); AI is not defined
regulatory_trigger: Using algorithmic recommendation technology to provide internet information services in mainland China; in force 1 March 2022
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling; Risk management; Human oversight; Data governance; Registration or filing; Prohibition
risk_tiers: Two levels: services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must file within 10 working days of launch and undergo security assessment (Arts. 24, 27); other services do not; Art. 23 also mandates a graded, categorised management system without naming tiers
enforcement_authority: The CAC coordinates; telecommunications, public security and market regulation departments supervise within their remits (Art. 3)
remedy_or_sanction: Sanctions under other laws and administrative regulations first; only where none applies, warning, criticism and rectification, then suspension of updates and a fine of RMB 10,000-100,000 for refusal or serious cases (Art. 31); some breaches go wholly to other rules (Art. 32); revocation of filing (Art. 33)
identified_gap: Users can switch off personalisation, delete tags and complain, but an explanation is owed only where an algorithm has an undefined 'major impact' on their rights and there is no right to human review of an outcome; the rules' own fine (up to RMB 100,000) is only a fallback where other laws are silent.
source_citation: Order No. 9 of the CAC, MIIT, MPS and SAMR, Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendation in Internet Information Services (adopted 16 November 2021, promulgated 31 December 2021, in force 1 March 2022)

instrument: Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis in Internet Information Services
original_title: 互联网信息服务深度合成管理规定
ai_systems_covered: Deep synthesis technology, i.e. deep learning, virtual reality and other generative or synthetic algorithms producing text, audio, images, video and virtual scenes (Art. 23); AI is not defined
regulatory_trigger: Providing deep synthesis services, or technical support for them, in mainland China; in force 10 January 2023
core_duties: Labelling; Risk management; Data governance; Registration or filing; Prohibition
risk_tiers: Services likely to confuse or mislead the public need prominent labels (Art. 17(1)); other services must offer a labelling function (Art. 17(2)); filing and security assessment for services with public-opinion or mobilisation capacity
enforcement_authority: The CAC coordinates; telecommunications and public security departments supervise within their remits (Arts. 3, 21)
remedy_or_sanction: Penalties under other laws and administrative regulations, heavier for serious consequences; orders to suspend services; public-security penalties or criminal liability (Arts. 21-22)
identified_gap: Sanctions are wholly borrowed from other laws, so there is no deepfake-specific penalty, and a person depicted in synthetic content gets no direct remedy beyond the consent prompt for biometric editing (Art. 14).
source_citation: Order No. 12 of the CAC, MIIT and MPS, Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis in Internet Information Services (adopted 3 November 2022, signed 25 November 2022, published 11 December 2022, in force 10 January 2023)

instrument: Interim Measures for the Administration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
original_title: 生成式人工智能服务管理暂行办法
ai_systems_covered: Generative AI technology, defined as models and related technology able to generate text, images, audio and video (Art. 22), used to serve the public in mainland China; R&D not offered to the public is excluded (Art. 2)
regulatory_trigger: Providing generative AI services, including via API, to the public in mainland China; in force 15 August 2023
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling; Risk management; Data governance; Registration or filing; Prohibition
risk_tiers: Two levels: services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity need security assessment and algorithm filing (Art. 17); other services do not; Arts. 3 and 16 envisage further classified, graded rules not yet set in the text
enforcement_authority: Cyberspace, development and reform, education, science and technology, industry and IT, public security, broadcasting and press-and-publication departments within their remits (Art. 16)
remedy_or_sanction: Penalties under the Cybersecurity, Data Security, Personal Information Protection and Science and Technology Progress Laws; otherwise warning, criticism, rectification and suspension of services (Art. 21)
identified_gap: It excludes R&D not offered to the public and leaves its promised graded rules to future instruments, so pre-release frontier-model development is largely outside its reach, and it carries no AI-specific fine.
source_citation: Order No. 15 of the CAC, NDRC, MoE, MoST, MIIT, MPS and NRTA, Interim Measures for the Administration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (adopted 23 May 2023, signed 10 July 2023, in force 15 August 2023)

instrument: Measures for Labelling AI-Generated Synthetic Content
original_title: 人工智能生成合成内容标识办法（国信办通字〔2025〕2号）
ai_systems_covered: AI-generated or synthetic text, images, audio, video and virtual scenes from services within the algorithm, deep synthesis and generative AI rules (Arts. 2-3); AI is not defined
regulatory_trigger: Providing generation or synthesis services, distributing content online, or listing apps that offer such services; in force 1 September 2025
core_duties: Labelling; Prohibition
enforcement_authority: Cyberspace, telecommunications, public security and radio and television departments within their remits (Art. 13)
remedy_or_sanction: No sanction of its own; breaches are handled under other laws, administrative regulations and departmental rules (Art. 13)
identified_gap: Implicit metadata labels are easily stripped as content moves between platforms, so traceability rests on platform detection and user self-declaration; issued by notice rather than as a numbered Order, it has no sanction clause of its own.
source_citation: CAC, MIIT, MPS and NRTA, Measures for Labelling AI-Generated Synthetic Content, Guoxinban Tongzi [2025] No. 2 (dated 7 March 2025, published 14 March 2025, in force 1 September 2025); with mandatory national standard GB 45438-2025 (issued 28 February 2025, in force 1 September 2025)

instrument: Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interactive Services
original_title: 人工智能拟人化互动服务管理暂行办法
ai_systems_covered: AI services offering the public sustained emotional interaction that simulates human personality, thinking and communication; customer service, Q&A, work, education and research services are excluded only where they involve no sustained emotional interaction (Art. 2); AI is not defined
regulatory_trigger: Offering such services to the public in mainland China; security assessment on launch, major change or reaching 1 million registered or 100,000 monthly active users (Art. 22); in force 15 July 2026
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling; Risk management; Audit; Data governance; Registration or filing; Prohibition
enforcement_authority: The CAC coordinates and NDRC, MIIT, MPS, SAMR and press-and-publication departments supervise within their remits (Art. 4); cyberspace, development-and-reform, industry-and-IT and public-security departments hold interview and penalty powers (Arts. 29-30); provincial cyberspace offices receive security assessments (Art. 22)
remedy_or_sanction: Penalties under relevant laws and administrative regulations first (Art. 1 cites the Cybersecurity, Data Security and Personal Information Protection Laws); where none applies, cyberspace, industry-and-IT and public-security departments may warn, criticise, order rectification and suspend registrations, and for refusal or serious cases order cessation with a fine of RMB 10,000-100,000, or RMB 100,000-200,000 where life or health is endangered and harm results (Art. 30)
identified_gap: Coverage turns on whether a service 'involves sustained emotional interaction', an undefined test that leaves general-purpose assistants used for companionship in uncertain territory; its own fines (up to RMB 200,000) apply only where no law provides, so deterrence rests on borrowed statutes.
source_citation: Order No. 21 of the CAC, NDRC, MIIT, MPS and SAMR, Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interactive Services (adopted 2 February 2026, promulgated 10 April 2026, in force 15 July 2026)

instrument: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 22 (automated individual decision-making, including profiling)
ai_systems_covered: Decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects; technology-neutral, so it reaches AI scoring and decision tools
regulatory_trigger: A controller takes a solely automated decision that produces legal or similarly significant effects for a person; applicable since 25 May 2018
core_duties: Prohibition; Transparency; Human oversight
enforcement_authority: National data protection supervisory authorities, with consistency ensured through the European Data Protection Board
remedy_or_sanction: Administrative fines up to EUR 20m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover (Art 83(5)); complaints, judicial remedies and compensation (Arts 77-82)
identified_gap: The 'solely automated' threshold and the contract, law and consent exceptions leave much decision-making supported by AI outside the rule, so nominal human involvement can defeat it. The Court of Justice has narrowed this gap by treating a decisive credit score as an automated decision (SCHUFA, C-634/21) and by requiring the logic of a decision to be explained (Dun & Bradstreet Austria, C-203/22).
source_citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, art 22 (with arts 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g), 15(1)(h))

instrument: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 35 (data protection impact assessment)
ai_systems_covered: Personal-data processing likely to pose a high risk, expressly including new technologies and systematic, extensive automated evaluation (profiling) on which significant decisions are based
regulatory_trigger: Before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals begins (Art 35(1), (3)); national supervisory-authority lists specify when an assessment is required
core_duties: Impact assessment; Risk management
enforcement_authority: National data protection supervisory authorities
remedy_or_sanction: Administrative fines up to EUR 10m or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (Art 83(4)); corrective orders under Art 58
identified_gap: The assessment is internal: it need not be published or shared with the people affected. Because the trigger is high-risk processing of personal data rather than AI use, AI systems that run on anonymised or non-personal data escape it.
source_citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, arts 35-36

instrument: Law Enforcement Directive, Article 11 (automated individual decision-making)
ai_systems_covered: Solely automated decisions, including profiling, taken by competent authorities for criminal-law purposes; technology-neutral, so it covers AI-based risk assessment
regulatory_trigger: A competent authority takes a solely automated decision with an adverse legal effect or significant effect on a person in preventing, investigating, detecting or prosecuting crime or executing penalties
core_duties: Prohibition; Human oversight
enforcement_authority: National supervisory authorities designated under the Directive (Art 41)
remedy_or_sanction: Penalties set by Member States (Art 57) and a right to compensation for damage (Art 56)
identified_gap: Beyond human intervention it leaves safeguards to national law, with no express right to an explanation or to contest, so protection against AI-driven policing varies by country and overlaps unclearly with the AI Act's law-enforcement high-risk category.
source_citation: Directive (EU) 2016/680 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by competent authorities for the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, and on the free movement of such data, OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 89, art 11

instrument: Digital Services Act
ai_systems_covered: Recommender, content-moderation and advertising systems of intermediary services, with extra duties for very large online platforms and search engines (45 million or more monthly EU users); not an AI-specific law
regulatory_trigger: Offering intermediary services to recipients in the Union; fully applicable since 17 Feb 2024, with very-large-platform duties applying four months after designation
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Audit; Human oversight
enforcement_authority: National Digital Services Coordinators; the European Commission for very large online platforms and search engines
remedy_or_sanction: Fines up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover and periodic penalty payments up to 5% of average daily turnover; compensation claims by recipients (Art 54)
identified_gap: It reaches AI only through recommender and moderation functions and requires disclosure of 'main parameters' rather than an auditable account of how a model behaves. For AI built into very large platforms, Commission supervision under the DSA now overlaps with the AI Office's exclusive AI Act competence added in 2026 (Art 75(1)(b) AI Act).
source_citation: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, arts 17, 20, 27, 34-35, 37-38

instrument: Artificial Intelligence Act
ai_systems_covered: Horizontal and risk-tiered: prohibited practices (Art 5, extended in 2026 to AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material), high-risk systems (Art 6, Annexes I and III), Art 50 transparency systems and general-purpose AI models (Chapter V)
regulatory_trigger: Placing on the market, putting into service or use of AI in the Union; phased: bans and AI literacy from 2 Feb 2025, GPAI duties from 2 Aug 2025, Art 50 from 2 Aug 2026, new bans from 2 Dec 2026, Annex III high-risk duties from 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I from 2 Aug 2028 (dates as amended by Reg (EU) 2026/1744)
core_duties: Prohibition; Risk management; Data governance; Human oversight; Transparency; Labelling; Impact assessment; Registration or filing
risk_tiers: Prohibited; High-risk; Transparency (limited) risk; Minimal; plus GPAI models and GPAI models with systemic risk
enforcement_authority: National market surveillance authorities; the Commission's AI Office for GPAI models and, since 2 Aug 2026, exclusively for providers of AI systems built on their own GPAI models (save listed exceptions such as Annex I products, critical infrastructure, law-enforcement and justice uses) and of AI in very large online platforms and search engines (Art 75(1)); the EDPS for EU institutions; the European AI Board coordinates
remedy_or_sanction: Fines up to EUR 35m or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices, EUR 15m or 3% for most other duties and EUR 7.5m or 1% for misleading information (Art 99), with lower caps for SMEs and, except for prohibited practices, small mid-caps; AI Office fines and periodic penalties for operators in its competence (Art 75c); Commission fines on GPAI providers (Art 101); withdrawal or recall
identified_gap: Affected persons get only a right to complain to a market surveillance authority (Art 85) and to an explanation of decisions based on Annex III high-risk outputs (Art 86), with no AI Act right to contest a decision or obtain compensation. The core high-risk regime is also deferred, to 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III and 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I systems.
source_citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024; as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (Digital Omnibus on AI), OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026

instrument: Platform Work Directive
ai_systems_covered: Automated monitoring and decision-making systems that digital labour platforms use to manage people performing platform work (algorithmic management); technology-neutral
regulatory_trigger: A digital labour platform uses automated monitoring or decision-making systems on people performing platform work; in force since 1 Dec 2024, with national transposition due by 2 Dec 2026 (Art 29)
core_duties: Prohibition; Data governance; Impact assessment; Transparency; Human oversight
enforcement_authority: Data protection authorities for the data-protection aspects of Arts 7-11, alongside labour and other competent authorities designated by each Member State (Art 24); no EU-level enforcer
remedy_or_sanction: Penalties set by Member States, with the GDPR Art 83(5) fine ceiling applying to breaches of Arts 7-11; dispute resolution and redress including compensation (Art 18)
identified_gap: It protects only people working through digital labour platforms, leaving algorithmic management in conventional workplaces outside its reach, and its practical content depends on national transposition due by 2 Dec 2026.
source_citation: Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on improving working conditions in platform work, OJ L, 2024/2831, 11.11.2024

instrument: Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
ai_systems_covered: AI systems used for the practices banned by Art 5 AI Act as first enacted, e.g. harmful manipulation, social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition at work or school, and real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement
regulatory_trigger: Placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system for an Art 5 practice; the bans have applied since 2 Feb 2025 and the fines since 2 Aug 2025
core_duties: Prohibition
enforcement_authority: National market surveillance authorities enforce Art 5, and the AI Office does so for systems within its exclusive competence (Art 75(1), as amended in 2026); the Commission issues the guidance
remedy_or_sanction: None in the guidelines; breaches of Art 5 carry fines up to EUR 35m or 7% of worldwide turnover (Art 99(3) AI Act)
identified_gap: Being non-binding, they cannot settle the contested edges of the bans (manipulation, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation), which only the Court of Justice can do. They also do not address the bans on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material added in 2026, which apply from 2 Dec 2026.
source_citation: European Commission, Communication C(2025) 5052 final of 29 July 2025, Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) (content approved on 4 February 2025, C(2025) 884 final)

instrument: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
ai_systems_covered: General-purpose AI models, with a Safety and Security chapter that applies only to models with systemic risk
regulatory_trigger: Voluntary signature by GPAI model providers; the underlying AI Act duties apply from 2 Aug 2025 (from 2 Aug 2027 for models already on the market), with Commission fining powers from 2 Aug 2026
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Data governance
risk_tiers: GPAI models; GPAI models with systemic risk
enforcement_authority: The AI Office of the European Commission
remedy_or_sanction: None for breach of the Code as such; GPAI providers face Commission fines up to EUR 15m or 3% of worldwide turnover under Art 101 AI Act
identified_gap: Adherence is voluntary and confers no presumption of conformity, only a recognised way to demonstrate compliance, so the practical content of the GPAI duties rests on AI Office enforcement discretion. Downstream deployers and affected people are protected only indirectly.
source_citation: European Commission (AI Office), General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, 10 July 2025; assessed as adequate by Commission Opinion C(2025) 5361 final of 1 August 2025

instrument: Commission Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of the AI Act
ai_systems_covered: AI systems that interact directly with people, generate or manipulate synthetic content, perform emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, or produce deep fakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest
regulatory_trigger: Art 50 duties apply from 2 Aug 2026; providers of generative systems placed on the market before then have until 2 Dec 2026 to meet the Art 50(2) marking duty (Art 111(4), inserted by Reg (EU) 2026/1744)
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling
enforcement_authority: National market surveillance authorities; the AI Office for provider duties of systems in its Art 75(1) competence (deployer duties only where it is also the deployer); the EDPS for EU institutions; the Commission issues the guidance
remedy_or_sanction: None in the guidelines; breaches of Art 50 carry fines up to EUR 15m or 3% of worldwide turnover (Art 99(4) AI Act)
identified_gap: Being non-binding, they cannot fix a technical benchmark for marking and detection, which is left to the voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (June 2026) and to future standards. Providers and deployers that do not sign the code must show compliance by other adequate means, assessed case by case by the competent authority.
source_citation: European Commission, Communication C(2026) 7702 final of 5 November 2026, Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the 'AI Act'), OJ C, C/2026/6005, 12.11.2026 (content approved on 20 July 2026, C(2026) 5054 final)

instrument: Digital Omnibus proposal (amendments to the GDPR and other data rules)
ai_systems_covered: Personal-data processing for developing and operating AI systems and models, and solely automated decisions under GDPR Art 22; refers to the AI Act definition of an AI system
regulatory_trigger: Would apply only once adopted; Council negotiating mandate agreed on 21 Oct 2026, Parliament still at committee stage on 19 Nov 2026, so trilogues have not begun
core_duties: Data governance
enforcement_authority: National data protection authorities and the European Data Protection Board (GDPR machinery unchanged)
remedy_or_sanction: GDPR sanctions machinery (Art 83 fines up to EUR 20m or 4% of turnover) would apply
identified_gap: As proposed it would ease AI training on personal data and recast Art 22 from a right into a list of permitted cases; the Council mandate restores the right-based Art 22 wording but refers to the ordinary Art 21 objection right instead of an unconditional one. With no Parliament position, the rules for AI-related processing remain unsettled.
source_citation: European Commission, Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulations (EU) 2016/679, (EU) 2018/1724, (EU) 2018/1725, (EU) 2023/2854 and Directives 2002/58/EC, (EU) 2022/2555 and (EU) 2022/2557 as regards the simplification of the digital legislative framework, and repealing Regulations (EU) 2018/1807, (EU) 2019/1150, (EU) 2022/868, and Directive (EU) 2019/1024 (Digital Omnibus), COM(2025) 837 final, 19.11.2025

instrument: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
ai_systems_covered: Any processing of digital personal data, including by AI systems; 'automated' is defined (s 2(b)) but AI is not named
regulatory_trigger: Processing digital personal data in India, or outside India when offering goods or services to people in India (s 3); phased: Board provisions from 13-11-2025, consent-manager provisions from 13-11-2026, most duties, rights and penalties from 13-05-2027 (G.S.R. 843(E))
core_duties: Transparency; Data governance; Impact assessment; Audit
enforcement_authority: Data Protection Board of India (ss 18-28), with appeals to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (s 29)
remedy_or_sanction: From 13-05-2027: penalties after Board inquiry under s 33 and the Schedule, up to INR 250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards; voluntary undertakings (s 32); blocking on the Board's reference (s 37)
identified_gap: It gives no right to an explanation of, human review of, or objection to an automated decision: s 8(3) asks only that the data feeding a decision be accurate and complete, and broad State and research exemptions (s 17) leave much public-sector AI outside its duties.
source_citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (Act 22 of 2023), Gazette of India Extraordinary Pt II s 1 (11 August 2023), ss 2(b), 3, 5, 8(3), 10-13, 17, 18-29, 33 and Schedule; commenced in phases by G.S.R. 843(E) (13 November 2025); ss 9(1) and 10(2)(c)(ii) modified by the Digital Personal Data Protection (Removal of Difficulties) Order 2026, S.O. 5458(E) (5 October 2026)

instrument: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025
ai_systems_covered: AI and machine-learning tools and techniques, designed in-house or procured, used by any SEBI-regulated person to serve investors or for internal, compliance or business purposes (reg 16C)
regulatory_trigger: Use of AI/ML tools by a SEBI-regulated person, whatever the scale of adoption; in force on gazette publication, 10-02-2025
core_duties: Data governance
enforcement_authority: Securities and Exchange Board of India (reg 16C(2))
remedy_or_sanction: Any action SEBI deems fit, including action under Chapter V of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations 2008
identified_gap: It fixes outcome liability on the regulated entity but prescribes no testing, bias control, explainability, human oversight or investor disclosure, which exist only in SEBI's unadopted June 2025 consultation paper; AI vendors are reached only through the entities that buy from them.
source_citation: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations 2025, F. No. SEBI/LAD-NRO/GN/2025/226 (6 February 2025), Gazette of India Extraordinary Pt III s 4 (10 February 2025), inserting Chapter IIIB (reg 16C) into the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations 2008

instrument: SEBI Master Circular for Stock Brokers, para 63 (Reporting for AI and ML applications and systems offered and used by market intermediaries)
ai_systems_covered: AI/ML applications that stock brokers offer to investors or use for trading, advice or compliance; Annexure-27 lists the technologies treated as AI/ML (an inclusive list); depository participants report under the parallel para 2.20 of the Master Circular for Depositories
regulatory_trigger: Offering or using an in-scope AI/ML application or system; quarterly reporting, a requirement first imposed by the circular of 4 January 2019
core_duties: Registration or filing
enforcement_authority: Securities and Exchange Board of India, with stock exchanges collecting and compiling the returns
remedy_or_sanction: None specific to the requirement; SEBI's general powers under the SEBI Act 1992
identified_gap: It builds an inventory for the regulator but imposes no testing, fairness, explainability or oversight duty and gives investors nothing to invoke; the parallel requirements for depositories, market infrastructure institutions and mutual funds follow the same reporting-only model.
source_citation: Securities and Exchange Board of India, Master Circular for Stock Brokers, SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/90 (17 June 2025), para 63 and Annexures 26-28, consolidating and (as it relates to stock brokers) rescinding Circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/DOS2/CIR/P/2019/10 (4 January 2019); for depository participants, Master Circular for Depositories, SEBI/HO/MRD/MRD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2024/168 (3 December 2024), para 2.20

instrument: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
ai_systems_covered: All digital personal data processing; the only algorithm-specific provision is r 13(3) on 'algorithmic software' used by Significant Data Fiduciaries; AI is not named
regulatory_trigger: Processing under the Act; rr 1, 2 and 17-21 in force 13-11-2025, r 4 (consent managers) from 13-11-2026, rr 3, 5-16, 22-23 (including r 13) from 13-05-2027; r 13 attaches on notification as a Significant Data Fiduciary
core_duties: Transparency; Data governance; Risk management; Impact assessment; Audit; Registration or filing
enforcement_authority: Data Protection Board of India
remedy_or_sanction: Penalties under s 33 and the Schedule of the parent Act (in force from 13-05-2027); the Rules add no sanction of their own
identified_gap: Rule 13(3) asks Significant Data Fiduciaries to check that algorithmic software is 'not likely to pose a risk' but sets no test, standard or audit method, and it binds only notified fiduciaries, so most AI deployers face no algorithm-specific duty.
source_citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025, G.S.R. 846(E), Gazette of India Extraordinary Pt II s 3(i) (13 November 2025), rr 1, 3, 4, 13, 14, made under s 40 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023

instrument: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026
ai_systems_covered: 'Synthetically generated information': realistic audio, visual or audio-visual content created or altered by computer (r 2(1)(wa)); routine edits excluded and text-only output outside the definition; AI itself is not defined
regulatory_trigger: Being an intermediary whose computer resource enables creating or sharing synthetic content (r 3(3)); significant social media intermediaries before publication (r 4(1A)); in force 20-02-2026
core_duties: Labelling; Transparency; Prohibition
enforcement_authority: No dedicated regulator: MeitY administers the Rules; takedown follows court orders or reasoned intimations from authorised officers (r 3(1)(d), as substituted by G.S.R. 775(E) and tightened in 2026); grievance officers and Grievance Appellate Committees hear complaints
remedy_or_sanction: Loss of safe-harbour protection under s 79(1) of the IT Act 2000 and liability under any law, including the IT Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (r 7)
identified_gap: Duties reach only intermediaries and only realistic audio-visual content, so AI-generated text and model developers that do not act as intermediaries fall outside, and the provenance duty applies only 'to the extent technically feasible'.
source_citation: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules 2026, G.S.R. 120(E), Gazette of India Extraordinary Pt II s 3(i) (10 February 2026), rr 2(1)(wa), 3(1)(c)-(d), 3(3), 4(1A), 7, as corrected by G.S.R. 148(E) (26 February 2026); amending the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021, G.S.R. 139(E) (25 February 2021), whose r 3(1)(d) was substituted by G.S.R. 775(E) (22 October 2025, w.e.f. 15 November 2025)

instrument: Ethical Guidelines for Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Research and Healthcare
ai_systems_covered: AI tools in biomedical research and healthcare, from development and validation to clinical deployment; the preamble quotes a descriptive, non-legal definition of AI
regulatory_trigger: None binding; applies to developing, validating or deploying health AI, chiefly through ethics-committee review of research proposals
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Impact assessment; Audit; Human oversight; Data governance
enforcement_authority: None; Indian Council of Medical Research guidance applied by institutional ethics committees
remedy_or_sanction: None; the compensation and grievance mechanisms it recommends are not enforceable through it
identified_gap: Because it is non-binding and aimed mainly at research ethics review, the patient rights and compensation it recommends are unenforceable, and commercial clinical AI tools are not brought under any licensing or liability regime by it.
source_citation: Indian Council of Medical Research, Ethical Guidelines for Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Research and Healthcare (DHR-ICMR, 2023), ISBN 978-93-5811-343-3

instrument: MeitY Advisory on Due Diligence by Intermediaries/Platforms under the IT Act 2000 and IT Rules 2021 (AI models and generative AI)
ai_systems_covered: AI models, large language models, generative AI, software and algorithms used on or offered through intermediaries, including tools that can create synthetic text, audio or video
regulatory_trigger: Using AI on or through an intermediary's computer resource, or making under-tested or unreliable AI available to users in India; compliance requested with immediate effect from 15-03-2024
core_duties: Labelling; Transparency; Prohibition
enforcement_authority: Issued by MeitY's Cyber Law and Data Governance Group; it names no enforcement body
remedy_or_sanction: None of its own; it reiterates that breaching the IT Act or IT Rules can lead to prosecution under the IT Act and criminal law
identified_gap: Its legal force is contested and its thresholds ('under-tested', 'unreliable') are undefined, so intermediaries cannot tell what binds them; its overlap with the binding 2026 synthetic-content rules is left unstated.
source_citation: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (Cyber Law and Data Governance Group), Advisory eNo.2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-3, 'Due diligence by Intermediaries / Platforms under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021' (15 March 2024), superseding the advisory of 1 March 2024

instrument: Report of the Committee to develop a Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI) in the Financial Sector
ai_systems_covered: AI, including generative and agentic AI, used by RBI-regulated entities such as banks and NBFCs; the glossary defines 'AI system' but not as law
regulatory_trigger: None binding; recommendations to RBI and regulated entities that take effect only if issued as RBI directions
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Audit; Human oversight; Data governance
risk_tiers: Low risk; Medium risk; High risk (recommended for each entity's board-approved AI policy, with human oversight for medium- and high-risk uses and third-party audits for high-risk ones)
enforcement_authority: Reserve Bank of India, only through its existing supervisory powers if it adopts the recommendations
remedy_or_sanction: None in the report
identified_gap: None of its 26 recommendations binds a regulated entity, so the consumer safeguards it proposes (being told when AI is used, grievance redress, escalation to a human) remain unenforceable; the RBI's only follow-up so far, the June 2026 model-risk guidance, is still a draft.
source_citation: Reserve Bank of India, Report of the Committee to develop a Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI) in the Financial Sector (13 August 2025), Press Release 2025-2026/902, paras 4.4.44, 4.4.49, 4.4.54-4.4.55 and Recommendations 16 and 18

instrument: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation
ai_systems_covered: AI systems across all sectors, approached through seven principles ('sutras') and six pillars; a non-statutory glossary defines 'AI system'
regulatory_trigger: None; voluntary adoption, with sector regulators applying existing laws
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Human oversight; Audit
enforcement_authority: None for the text; MeitY is the nodal ministry and sector regulators enforce their own laws; the coordinating group it proposed was set up in April 2026 in modified form as the AI Governance and Economic Group, chaired by the IT Minister rather than the Principal Scientific Adviser and without sector regulators as members
remedy_or_sanction: None; compliance is voluntary
identified_gap: It states that a separate AI law is not needed at this stage and defers risk classification and liability allocation to future work, so no developer or deployer faces an enforceable duty under it; press reports say MeitY announced in October 2026 a regulation-focused consultation paper, unpublished at 19-11-2026.
source_citation: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (5 November 2025, released with PIB Release ID 2186639)

instrument: Consultation Paper on Guidelines for Responsible Usage of AI/ML in Indian Securities Markets
ai_systems_covered: AI/ML applications and models used by SEBI-regulated market participants such as exchanges, brokers and mutual funds; Annexure A gives descriptive, non-legal definitions of AI and ML
regulatory_trigger: Would apply to market participants' use of AI/ML once final guidelines issue; comments closed 11-07-2025 and no final guidelines had been issued by 19-11-2026
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Audit; Human oversight; Data governance
risk_tiers: Client-impacting business uses (full framework); other uses such as internal compliance, surveillance and cybersecurity (regulatory-lite)
enforcement_authority: Securities and Exchange Board of India
remedy_or_sanction: None while a proposal; SEBI's powers under the SEBI Act 1992 would apply if adopted
identified_gap: More than a year after consultation closed it remains unadopted, so the only binding SEBI rule on AI conduct is reg 16C's bare liability clause; its tiers follow the purpose of use rather than model risk.
source_citation: Securities and Exchange Board of India, Consultation Paper on Guidelines for Responsible Usage of AI/ML in Indian Securities Markets (20 June 2025), paras 5-6 and Annex A

instrument: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (draft)
ai_systems_covered: Intermediaries generally; the AI-relevant proposals are a continuous on-screen label for visual synthetic content and a duty to obey written MeitY advisories, including those on AI
regulatory_trigger: Would apply from a commencement date left blank in the draft; first draft published 30-03-2026, revised draft and a comment deadline of 07-05-2026 announced on 21-04-2026; not notified as of 19-11-2026
core_duties: Labelling
enforcement_authority: MeitY for Part II duties; the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting's Part III oversight mechanism for news and current-affairs content
remedy_or_sanction: Would put s 79 safe harbour at risk for ignoring MeitY advisories; no new penalty
identified_gap: Draft r 3(4) would make compliance with written MeitY advisories, SOPs and codes a condition of safe harbour; although each must state its legal basis and be consistent with the Act, executive guidance would gain binding effect without parliamentary scrutiny or any process for challenging a particular advisory.
source_citation: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules 2026, revised draft notification (April 2026), draft paras 3 (r 3(3)(a)(ii)), 4 (r 3(4)), 5 (r 8) and 6 (r 14); first draft published 30 March 2026; MeitY Notice of 21 April 2026 (comments by 7 May 2026)

instrument: Draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026
ai_systems_covered: All models used by RBI-regulated entities, including AI/ML, generative, foundational, frontier and third-party models; 'model' is defined, AI is not
regulatory_trigger: Would apply to model use by banks, NBFCs and other listed regulated entities once finalised; comments closed 24-07-2026 and it remained a draft as of 19-11-2026
core_duties: Risk management; Human oversight; Transparency; Audit; Data governance
risk_tiers: Entity-defined risk tiers based on materiality and complexity (including a 'high' tier needing Board-committee review); AI models also tiered by reliance and autonomy
enforcement_authority: Reserve Bank of India (Department of Regulation)
remedy_or_sanction: None specified; it would rely on RBI's supervisory powers, and existing RBI Directions prevail where inconsistent
identified_gap: Customer protection is limited to disclosure that AI is in use, an option to reach a human and existing grievance channels, with no right to an explanation of an individual decision; further AI-specific requirements are left for later.
source_citation: Reserve Bank of India, Draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management 2026 (24 June 2026), Press Release 2026-2027/528, paras 4-6, 17-25, 49-63

instrument: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI)
original_title: 個人情報の保護に関する法律（平成15年法律第57号）
ai_systems_covered: Any handling of personal information, including AI training and automated analysis; no AI-specific rules beyond the 2026 consent exemption for statistical uses, which covers AI development
regulatory_trigger: Acquiring, using or providing personal information; the 2026 amendment commences in stages: some penalty provisions on 17 January 2027, the rest on a date set by Cabinet Order within two years of promulgation (17 July 2026)
core_duties: Transparency; Data governance; Prohibition; Registration or filing
enforcement_authority: Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC)
remedy_or_sanction: PPC recommendations and orders backed by criminal penalties; the 2026 amendment adds administrative surcharges equal to the benefit obtained from serious, large-scale violations (Art. 148-3 et seq., not yet in force)
identified_gap: Provides no right to explanation or human review of automated decisions and no impact assessment for AI uses, even as the 2026 amendment removes consent for personal data used only for statistical purposes, including AI development.
source_citation: Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Act No. 57 of 30 May 2003 (Japan), as amended (official translation current to Act No. 37 of 2021); Act Partially Amending the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and Other Acts, Act No. 56 of 2026, promulgated 17 July 2026 (text published by the PPC: https://www.ppc.go.jp/files/pdf/260717_houritsu.pdf)

instrument: Copyright Act, Article 30-4 (Exploitation without the Purpose of Enjoying the Thoughts or Sentiments Expressed in a Work)
original_title: 著作権法（昭和45年法律第48号）第30条の4
ai_systems_covered: Use of copyrighted works for data analysis and other non-enjoyment purposes, including AI training; no system categories
regulatory_trigger: Exploiting a work where enjoying its expression is not the purpose (e.g. data analysis for AI training); in force 1 January 2019
enforcement_authority: No regulator named; rights holders enforce in the courts (the Agency for Cultural Affairs issues only interpretive guidance)
remedy_or_sanction: Injunction, damages and criminal penalties under the Copyright Act where a use falls outside the exception
identified_gap: Permits training broadly but gives rights holders no notice, opt-out or disclosure mechanism, and its 'unreasonable prejudice' limit is clarified mainly by non-binding agency guidance.
source_citation: Copyright Act, Act No. 48 of 6 May 1970 (Japan), Art. 30-4 (inserted by Act No. 30 of 2018); official translation, Japanese Law Translation Database System (Ministry of Justice), current to Act No. 52 of 2021

instrument: Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-related Technology (AI Promotion Act)
original_title: 人工知能関連技術の研究開発及び活用の推進に関する法律（令和7年法律第53号）
ai_systems_covered: All 'artificial intelligence-related technology', defined functionally in Art. 2; no system categories
regulatory_trigger: Developing, providing or using AI in business (Art. 7); in force on promulgation (4 June 2025), with Chapters III-IV (Basic Plan, Strategic Headquarters) from 1 September 2025
enforcement_authority: None with enforcement power; the AI Strategic Headquarters coordinates and may request cooperation (Arts. 19-20, 25), and the national government may give guidance and advice (Art. 16)
remedy_or_sanction: None; the Act contains no fines, orders or other sanctions
identified_gap: Creates no enforceable duties, sanctions or individual remedies for private developers or deployers, whom Art. 7 does not distinguish and asks only to cooperate, so AI harms depend on other laws. Coded Binding as a statute although its business-facing provisions are hortatory; a government working group's draft outline (18 November 2026) proposes legislation imposing safety and reporting duties, orders and penalties on providers of high-capability AI, but nothing has been decided or amended.
source_citation: Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-related Technology, Act No. 53 of 4 June 2025 (Japan), Arts. 1-28 and Supplementary Provisions; official translation, Japanese Law Translation Database System (Ministry of Justice)

instrument: General Understanding on AI and Copyright in Japan
original_title: AIと著作権に関する考え方について
ai_systems_covered: AI training on copyrighted works, generation and use of outputs, and copyrightability of AI-generated material; no system categories
regulatory_trigger: Using copyrighted works to develop or train AI, or generating and using outputs similar to existing works
enforcement_authority: None; compiled by the Legal Subcommittee of the Copyright Subdivision, Council for Cultural Affairs; courts decide infringement
remedy_or_sanction: None of its own; infringement remedies under the Copyright Act apply
identified_gap: Expressly not legally binding and not a definitive legal assessment, so it gives developers and rights holders no legal certainty and creates no disclosure or opt-out mechanism.
source_citation: Legal Subcommittee, Copyright Subdivision, Council for Cultural Affairs, General Understanding on AI and Copyright in Japan (AIと著作権に関する考え方について), 15 March 2024; English overview, Agency for Cultural Affairs, May 2024 (https://www.bunka.go.jp/english/policy/copyright/pdf/94055801_01.pdf)

instrument: AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.2)
original_title: AI事業者ガイドライン（第1.2版）
ai_systems_covered: AI systems and services across the lifecycle, including advanced AI, AI agents and physical AI; defines 'AI system' for its own purposes while noting AI has no agreed definition
regulatory_trigger: Developing, providing or using AI in business activities; voluntary, with no commencement date
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling; Risk management; Human oversight; Data governance
enforcement_authority: None; issued jointly by MIC and METI as a living document
remedy_or_sanction: None
identified_gap: Entirely voluntary with no verification, reporting or enforcement mechanism, and its developer, provider and business-user roles are not tied to legal liability for harm.
source_citation: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications and Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.2, 31 March 2026; provisional English translation

instrument: Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety (Version 1.20)
original_title: AIセーフティに関する評価観点ガイド（第1.20版）
ai_systems_covered: LLM-based systems and, from v1.20, AI agent systems, with image (multimodal) examples; borrows the AI Guidelines for Business definition of 'AI system'
regulatory_trigger: Voluntary safety evaluation by AI developers and providers; v1.20 published 7 July 2026
core_duties: Risk management; Audit; Transparency; Data governance
enforcement_authority: None; published by the Japan AI Safety Institute (J-AISI)
remedy_or_sanction: None
identified_gap: A voluntary method with no pass/fail criteria and no duty to evaluate or disclose results; v1.20 still limits its scope mainly to direct impacts on end users and the external environments a system accesses, leaving socio-technical harms to further study.
source_citation: Japan AI Safety Institute, Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety (AIセーフティに関する評価観点ガイド), Ver. 1.20, 7 July 2026 (Japanese only; earlier versions 18 September 2024 and 28 March 2025)

instrument: Guideline for Ensuring the Appropriateness of Research & Development and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technology
original_title: 人工知能関連技術の研究開発及び活用の適正性確保に関する指針
ai_systems_covered: All AI-related technology within the AI Promotion Act; risk-based approach without tiers; covers overseas businesses providing AI in Japan
regulatory_trigger: Research, development, provision or use of AI; adopted by the AI Strategic Headquarters on 19 December 2025 under Art. 13 of the AI Promotion Act
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling; Risk management; Human oversight; Data governance
enforcement_authority: None; the guideline is to be reviewed continuously
remedy_or_sanction: None
identified_gap: Expressly declines to give a single definition or standard of 'appropriateness' and relies on voluntary effort, so no duty can be derived or enforced and affected persons gain no rights.
source_citation: Artificial Intelligence Strategic Headquarters, Guideline for Ensuring the Appropriateness of Research & Development and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technology, decision of 19 December 2025, under Art. 13 of Act No. 53 of 2025; provisional English translation, Cabinet Office

instrument: Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan (Second Plan: “Japan AI Transformation; A Stronger Nation. Greater Prosperity.”)
ai_systems_covered: Government AI policy on deployment, development, governance and society; no system categories
regulatory_trigger: Cabinet decision under Art. 18 of the AI Promotion Act: first plan 23 December 2025, second plan 14 July 2026; the plan itself says it will be revised as needed, in principle annually
enforcement_authority: None with enforcement power; the AI Strategic Headquarters drafts the plan and promotes and follows up its implementation (Art. 20)
remedy_or_sanction: None
identified_gap: Defers rather than resolves the core regulatory question: it promises continuous review of the AI Act and legal analysis of rights infringements but sets no timetable, mechanism or sanction for enforceable duties.
source_citation: Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan (Second), Cabinet Decision of 14 July 2026, under Art. 18(1) of Act No. 53 of 2025 (first plan: Cabinet Decision of 23 December 2025); provisional English translation, Cabinet Office

instrument: Principle Code for the Protection of Intellectual Property and Transparency for the Appropriate Use of Generative AI
original_title: 生成AIの適切な利活用等に向けた知的財産の保護及び透明性に関するプリンシプル・コード
ai_systems_covered: Generative AI systems and services provided to the public in Japan, including by overseas businesses; defines 'generative AI' and its developers and providers for its own scope
regulatory_trigger: Providing a generative AI system or service to the public in Japan; acceptance notifications to the Cabinet Office opened 26 October 2026
core_duties: Transparency; Labelling; Risk management; Data governance; Registration or filing
enforcement_authority: Cabinet Office Intellectual Property Strategy Promotion Office receives and lists acceptance notifications without reviewing their content
remedy_or_sanction: None; comply-or-explain, with reputational consequences only
identified_gap: Disclosure is comply-or-explain, and rights holders may request only limited information (such as whether specific URLs were used) and only when in or preparing legal proceedings, so they have no enforceable route to learn how their works were used.
source_citation: Cabinet Office Intellectual Property Strategy Promotion Office, Principle Code for the Protection of Intellectual Property and Transparency for the Appropriate Use of Generative AI, published 25 August 2026 on the Intellectual Property Strategy Headquarters website after review by the AI-era IP Study Group (13th meeting, 18 August 2026); provisional English translation, Cabinet Office (Japanese text: https://www.cas.go.jp/jp/seisakukaigi/titeki2/ai_kentoukai/kaisai/pdf/ai_principle_code.pdf)

instrument: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
ai_systems_covered: Any processing of personal data, by automated means or not, which captures AI systems that process personal data; AI is never named
regulatory_trigger: Processing personal data where the controller or processor operates in Nigeria, the processing occurs in Nigeria, or the data subject is in Nigeria (s 2)
core_duties: Transparency; Impact assessment; Data governance; Registration or filing
enforcement_authority: Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
remedy_or_sanction: NDPC enforcement orders, including compensation and penalties up to the greater of N10m or 2% of prior-year gross revenue (major importance) or N2m or 2% (others) (s 48); offence of ignoring a compliance order, fine or up to 1 year's imprisonment (s 49); civil damages (s 51)
identified_gap: The Act never mentions AI and does not separate developers from deployers, so it reaches AI only through personal-data processing and leaves AI built on anonymised or non-personal data outside its duties.
source_citation: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (Act No 37), Official Gazette No 119, Vol 110 (1 July 2023), ss 2, 24, 27, 28, 44, 48

instrument: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, s 37 (automated decision-making)
ai_systems_covered: Decisions based solely on automated processing of personal data, including profiling, that produce legal or similarly significant effects
regulatory_trigger: A controller takes a decision about a data subject based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects
core_duties: Human oversight
enforcement_authority: Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
remedy_or_sanction: Borrowed from the same Act: NDPC enforcement orders and penalties (s 48; up to the greater of N10m or 2% of prior-year gross revenue for major-importance controllers), offence of ignoring a compliance order (s 49), civil damages (s 51)
identified_gap: The right is an opt-out with wide exceptions (contract, written law, consent), and although ss 27(1)(g) and 34 require notice of the significance and consequences of automated decisions, nothing gives the person the logic of their own decision, so they contest outcomes they cannot see into.
source_citation: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (Act No 37), s 37; see also ss 27(1)(g), 34(1)(a)(viii)

instrument: Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025
ai_systems_covered: Emerging technologies 'such as Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things and Blockchain' used to process personal data, plus profiling and automated decisions (Arts 28, 43-44)
regulatory_trigger: Deploying or planning to deploy AI or other emerging technologies to process personal data; listed DPIAs must be filed before processing starts (Arts 28(3), 28(9), 43); issued 20 March 2025, applied from 19 September 2025
core_duties: Risk management; Impact assessment; Data governance; Registration or filing; Prohibition
enforcement_authority: Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
remedy_or_sanction: None of its own; relies on NDPA Part X (s 48), and a failed DPIA may also lead to restriction of the controller's platforms (Art 28(6))
identified_gap: AI appears only as an example of 'emerging technologies', with no definition or threshold; the core design duty is phrased as an expectation (Art 43(2)) and the duty to stop using a system turns on the controller's own judgement (Art 44(3)), so it is unclear when an AI deployment crosses the line.
source_citation: Nigeria Data Protection Commission, Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 (NDPC/NDP ACT-GAID/01/2025, 20 March 2025), arts 8-9, 28, 40, 43-44

instrument: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy
ai_systems_covered: AI across the economy; five pillars, including responsible and ethical AI and a robust AI governance framework
regulatory_trigger: None; a 'living document' setting strategies to be implemented over five years
enforcement_authority: None named; the Ministry leads, with an AI governance regulatory system to be promoted by NITDA
remedy_or_sanction: None
identified_gap: It promises principles, a risk-management framework and an AI governance regulatory body but creates no enforceable duty, right or sanction, so delivery depends on legislation and NITDA instruments that are not yet in force.
source_citation: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (September 2025)

instrument: National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill 2025
ai_systems_covered: Any AI system developed, deployed, placed on the market or used in Nigeria, by private persons or public institutions; NITDA may classify AI by risk through later regulation (ss 2(d), 63-65, 83)
regulatory_trigger: Developing, deploying, marketing, operating or making available an AI system used or relied on in Nigeria (s 83); would apply only on enactment, and no Senate passage or assent had been reported by 19-11-2026
core_duties: Transparency; Risk management; Impact assessment; Audit; Human oversight; Data governance
enforcement_authority: National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), as the 'Regulatory Agency', cooperating with the NDPC (ss 64(1)(j), 66-68, 83)
remedy_or_sanction: Enforcement orders to remedy, compensate, account for profits or pay up to the higher of N10m or 2% of prior-year Nigerian gross revenue; suspension of seriously risky systems; civil liability (ss 67-68)
identified_gap: The Bill leaves the risk classes and most detailed obligations to future NITDA regulations, and while it tells AI agents to cooperate with the NDPC it sets no mechanism for resolving clashes between NITDA, the NDPC and sectoral regulators.
source_citation: National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill 2025 (National Assembly), Pt XI ss 63-69, Pt XII ss 70-79, s 83
